questions.question: What historical view of the Earth was common before modern astronomy, regarding its shape and the motion of celestial bodies?
options: It was thought to be a sphere, remaining perfectly still while only the Moon moved around it.
It was once thought to be flat, with the Sun and all the stars moving around it.
It was believed to be a cube that rotated on a fixed axis once a year.
It was thought to be a hollow cylinder orbiting a central fire.

questions.question: Until which century did most people believe that the Earth was situated at the very centre of the universe?
options: The 12th century
The 20th century
The 16th century
The 18th century

questions.question: At what angle is the axis of the Earth tilted as it spins?
options: 12.5 degrees
23.5 degrees
45.0 degrees
90.0 degrees

questions.question: How does the mass of an object affect the strength of its gravitational pull?
options: The greater the mass, the stronger the gravity.
The greater the mass, the weaker the gravity.
Mass does not affect gravity, only the object's temperature does.
Gravity remains completely constant regardless of mass.

questions.question: What effect does Earth's gravity have on the Moon to keep it in orbit?
options: It pushes the Moon further away into deep space, preventing it from colliding.
It pulls the Moon towards the centre of Earth, changing its direction and causing it to orbit.
It heats the Moon's surface, creating a thermal current that propels it.
It causes the Moon to spin rapidly on its own axis every 24 hours.

questions.question: How does the angle of heating affect how effectively a surface is warmed?
options: Heating a surface at a shallow angle is far more effective than heating it from directly overhead.
Heating a surface is equally effective at all angles of contact.
Heating a surface from directly overhead is more effective than heating it at a different angle.
Heating is only effective when the source is below the surface.

questions.question: What happens to rays of light when they hit a surface face-on compared to hitting it at an angle?
options: They are less spread out than if they hit at an angle.
They are more spread out than if they hit at an angle.
They disappear completely upon impact.
They bounce off without transferring any heat energy.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what a star is?
options: A small solid rock that reflects light from nearby planets.
An extremely large sphere of hot gas that gives out light.
A cold, dusty cloud that blocks light from the Sun.
A frozen liquid sphere orbiting a moon.

questions.question: What does our solar system consist of?
options: Only the Earth and the Moon.
A collection of distant galaxies that do not contain stars.
The Sun and all of the objects that orbit it.
A cluster of stars that do not have any planets orbiting them.

questions.question: How do the distances between objects in our solar system compare to the actual sizes of those objects?
options: The distances are very, very large compared to the sizes of the objects.
The distances are nearly identical to the diameters of the planets.
The objects are so close together that they constantly touch.
The distances are extremely small compared to the sizes of the objects.

questions.question: Why do countries located near the Equator not experience distinct summer and winter seasons?
options: They stay close to 'face-on' to the Sun all year round.
They are completely shielded from the Sun's rays by the atmosphere.
They tilt dramatically away from the Sun every six months.
They orbit a different star than the rest of the Earth.

questions.question: Why do the stars in the night sky appear so much smaller and dimmer than our Sun?
options: They are made of cold solid ice instead of hot gas.
They are much further away than our Sun.
They are actually located inside Earth's atmosphere.
They only emit light during the daytime.

questions.question: What is a light-year, and why is it used in astronomy?
options: It is the time it takes for Earth to orbit the Sun, used to measure planetary ages.
It is the distance light travels in one year, making it suitable for measuring vast distances in space.
It is the brightness of a star over a twelve-month period, used to classify star types.
It is the distance from the Earth to the Moon, used to measure local orbits.

questions.question: What is a galaxy?
options: A group of planets orbiting a single dwarf star.
A collection of billions of stars grouped together in the universe.
A belt of asteroids located between Mars and Jupiter.
A single massive star that has run out of fuel.

questions.question: What is the shape of Earth's orbit around the Sun?
options: A highly elongated, long oval shape.
An almost perfect circle.
A spiral that gets closer to the Sun every year.
A perfect square with rounded corners.

questions.question: Which of the following explains why the Moon appears to change shape over time?
options: The Moon physically expands and contracts due to temperature changes.
The Moon orbits the Earth about once per month (27.3 days).
The Moon passes through Earth's atmosphere, which blocks its light.
The Moon spins on its axis once every hour.
